title: WISE 0855
blurb: The coldest brown dwarf known. Too faint for one exposure — until they are added up.
story: WISE 0855 is the coldest brown dwarf known: colder than ice, and only about 7 light-years away. In a single two-minute SPHEREx exposure it barely rises out of the noise. Here every visit's exposures are added together, and a faint dot appears in the cross-hair. Blink the visits: it steps toward the west, about 8 arcseconds a year. Blink X found it by itself this way; even ESA's Gaia star catalogue does not list it.

spectrum.hint: It is faint: every dot is one noisy exposure, so the line joins the middle value of each 9 neighbouring measurements. From 3.82 to 4.41 µm it gets brighter toward longer wavelengths, about 2.2 times. Very cool objects do that.

doodles.explain: Too faint to stand out in a single exposure, this one appears when each visit's exposures are added together. It slides steadily toward the west: 8.2 arcseconds (1.3 SPHEREx pixels) in 12 months, about 8.2 arcseconds a year. Steady drift like this is how a nearby star or brown dwarf looks from Earth. (Something this close also wobbles with the seasons, by up to an arcsecond: over a year or so that wobble is part of the number.) This is WISEA J085510.74-071442.5, a known brown dwarf (SIMBAD). The catalogue lists 8.15 arcseconds a year; these images give 8.2 ± 0.6.

full_spectrum.hint: It shows up only from 3.8 to 5.0 µm. In the other colour bands nothing sits on its spot: the hollow dots there are light from a neighbour 6″ away that reaches into the measuring circle. That neighbour also adds a little to the object's own dots. It is brightest near 4.5 µm, at about 0.6 mJy. All of it was measured in one visit, 2025-10-31 to 2025-11-14.

source: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (collections spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3)
